enrichment.method: Original topic-specific reading prompts connect the cited source to equations, tensor shapes, examples, assumptions, comparison design, and limitations. They do not claim that toy examples are experiments reported by the papers.

issues.before: For T dispatched tokens, k assignments, hidden width d, and b bytes per activation value
issues.after: For T input tokens, k selected experts per token, hidden width d, and b bytes per activation value
issues.reason: Defines T before replication and k per token so the kT payload formula cannot be read as counting dispatched assignments twice.

issues.before: Flattening that grid produces a vector, but nearby coordinates no longer visibly express the original spatial arrangement.
issues.after: Flattening preserves all pixel values when the original shape and ordering are known. What changes is the representation: a generic dense layer does not automatically exploit the image's two-dimensional neighborhood structure.
issues.reason: Separates an invertible reshape from the architectural inductive bias; flattening alone does not destroy spatial information.

issues.before: Each output channel combines information from all input channels within the kernel footprint.
issues.after: In a standard ungrouped convolution, each output channel combines all input channels within the kernel footprint. Grouped and depthwise convolutions restrict those channel connections.
issues.reason: The all-input-channel statement applies to groups=1, not to every convolution.

issues.before: Appending CLS gives [B, 197, 768].
issues.after: Prepending CLS, as in the original ViT, gives [B, 197, 768].
issues.reason: Corrects the placement of the original ViT classification token; the sequence shape is unchanged.

issues.before: Without spatial position information, a standard self-attention stack cannot distinguish arbitrary permutations of otherwise identical patch embeddings in the intended image layout.
issues.after: Without positional information, standard self-attention is permutation-equivariant: reordering patch tokens reorders their token-level outputs. A mean-pooled or fixed-CLS image representation is invariant to that reordering, so patch content alone does not specify the spatial layout.
issues.reason: Distinguishes equivariant token outputs from invariant pooled or CLS outputs instead of implying that all outputs are unchanged by permutations.

issues.before: Promptable segmentation uses user-specified spatial cues to identify a region, and video segmentation additionally requires memory across frames.
issues.after: Promptable segmentation uses spatial cues to identify a region; SAM 2 uses temporal memory to maintain the selected object across video frames.
issues.reason: Attributes streaming memory to SAM 2 rather than claiming every video-segmentation architecture must use memory.

issues.before: Changing the tokenizer changes token IDs and segmentation, so an embedding table trained for one vocabulary cannot generally interpret another. Inspect exact tokenization for spaces, Unicode, numbers, and code before interpreting length or errors. Different tokenizers can produce different perplexities on the same text because the prediction units differ. Longer vocabularies may shorten sequences but enlarge embeddings and output projections, making tokenization an architectural and systems trade-off.
issues.after: Changing the tokenizer changes token IDs and segmentation, so an embedding table trained for one vocabulary cannot generally interpret another. Inspect exact tokenization for spaces, Unicode, numbers, and code before interpreting length or errors. Different tokenizers can produce different perplexities on the same text because the prediction units differ. Larger vocabularies may shorten tokenized sequences but enlarge the embedding table and output projection, making tokenization an architectural and systems trade-off.
issues.reason: Clarify vocabulary size rather than token length.
issues.origin: Claude baseline finding validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: For [BOS, A, B, EOS], one explicit training pair uses inputs [BOS, A, B] and targets [A, B, EOS]. Logits have shape [B, T−1, V], with one V-way classification problem per valid target. Some model APIs accept the full sequence as both input and labels and perform the shift internally; others expect pre-shifted tensors. Applying both conventions shifts twice. Check the interface with a tiny sequence whose expected targets you can list by hand.
issues.after: For [BOS, A, B, EOS], one explicit training pair uses inputs [BOS, A, B] and targets [A, B, EOS]. Here T = 4 is the full sequence length, leaving T−1 = 3 target positions. For N_batch such examples, logits have shape [N_batch, T−1, V], with one V-way classification problem per valid target. Some model APIs accept the full sequence as both input and labels and perform the shift internally; others expect pre-shifted tensors. Applying both conventions shifts twice. Check the interface with a tiny sequence whose expected targets you can list by hand.
issues.reason: Avoid using B for both a token name and the batch dimension.

issues.before: GPT-style models are associated with causal decoding, while BERT uses bidirectional encoding trained with a masked-token objective. LLaMA is also a causal decoder family, so its differences from GPT are often block-level and training-design choices rather than a different autoregressive factorization. Family names span multiple releases; a careful comparison names the exact paper or checkpoint instead of assuming one configuration describes every descendant.
issues.after: GPT-style models are associated with causal decoding, while original BERT uses bidirectional encoding pretrained with masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction. LLaMA is also a causal decoder family, so its differences from GPT are often block-level and training-design choices rather than a different autoregressive factorization. Family names span multiple releases; a careful comparison names the exact paper or checkpoint instead of assuming one configuration describes every descendant.
issues.reason: Include both original BERT pretraining objectives without generalizing to every later encoder.
issues.origin: Claude baseline finding validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: BERT reads bidirectionally and predicts masked tokens, whereas LLaMA uses causal next-token prediction. Both GPT-style decoders and LLaMA use causal generation, so their differences can center on normalization, position encoding, FFNs, data, and training choices.

Both GPT-style decoders and LLaMA use causal generation, so their differences can center on normalization, position encoding, FFNs, data, and training choices.

issues.before: Temperature divides logits by a positive value before softmax: lower temperature sharpens probabilities, while higher temperature flattens them. Top-k keeps a fixed number of highest-scoring candidates. Top-p keeps a smallest high-probability prefix whose cumulative probability reaches a chosen threshold, so its candidate count adapts to uncertainty. After filtering, probabilities must be renormalized. Greedy decoding is a limiting or separate selection rule; literally dividing by temperature zero is undefined.
issues.after: Temperature divides logits by a positive value before softmax: lower temperature sharpens probabilities, while higher temperature flattens them. Top-k keeps a fixed number of highest-scoring candidates. Top-p keeps a smallest high-probability prefix whose cumulative probability reaches a chosen threshold, so its candidate count adapts to uncertainty. After filtering, probabilities must be renormalized. Greedy decoding is a limiting or separate selection rule; literally dividing by temperature zero is undefined. Positive temperature scaling preserves the ranking and therefore top-k membership, but it can change the top-p nucleus. When combining controls, report whether temperature is applied before truncation.
issues.reason: Clarify the interaction of temperature and probability-mass truncation; positive scaling preserves order.
issues.origin: Claude baseline finding validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: Use four experts with d = 16 and h = 32. Each two-matrix expert has 1,024 weight parameters, so the collection has 4,096. Route a batch of token vectors, run only selected experts, and restore the original token order before the residual addition. A useful debugging test sends every token to one chosen expert and checks that the layer matches that standalone MLP. A frequent error is returning tokens in dispatch order, which silently mixes representations between sequence positions while leaving tensor shapes apparently valid.
issues.after: Use four experts with d = 16 and h = 32. Each two-matrix expert has 1,024 weight parameters, so the collection has 4,096. Route a batch of token vectors, run only selected experts, and restore the original token order before the residual addition. A useful debugging test sends every token to one chosen expert and checks that the MoE contribution, before residual addition, equals the standalone MLP output multiplied by its gate weight. Exact equality to the unweighted MLP requires a gate of one. A frequent error is returning tokens in dispatch order, which silently mixes representations between sequence positions while leaving tensor shapes apparently valid.
issues.reason: A correct Switch-style top-one layer retains its selected probability multiplier; ignoring that gate creates a false debugging failure.
issues.origin: Claude baseline finding validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: Suppose a router produces probabilities [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]. A top-two rule chooses experts zero and one. If selected weights are renormalized, their weights become 0.6875 and 0.3125. If they are not, their total contribution remains scaled by 0.8. Those are different layer definitions. During debugging, log logits, selected indices, gate weights, and per-expert token counts. Extreme logits early in training can make assignments overly concentrated, while perfectly balanced counts alone do not prove that routing improves task quality.
issues.after: Suppose a router produces probabilities [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]. Using zero-based indexing, a top-two rule chooses experts at indices 0 and 1. If selected weights are renormalized, their weights become 0.6875 and 0.3125. If they are not, their total contribution remains scaled by 0.8. Those are different layer definitions. During debugging, log logits, selected indices, gate weights, and per-expert token counts. Extreme logits early in training can make assignments overly concentrated, while perfectly balanced counts alone do not prove that routing improves task quality.
issues.reason: Make the indexing convention explicit.
issues.origin: Claude baseline finding validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: Experts one and two. Their selected mass is 0.8, so the weights are 0.625 and 0.375.
issues.after: The experts at zero-based indices 1 and 2, namely the second and third experts with probabilities 0.5 and 0.3. Their selected mass is 0.8, so the weights are 0.625 and 0.375.
issues.reason: Remove ambiguity between expert indices and ordinal positions.

issues.before: A common top-one balancing term uses f_e, the fraction of tokens assigned to expert e, and P_e, the mean routing probability for e across the batch. The product sum penalizes concentration when assignment frequency and probability mass align. A coefficient sets the strength of this auxiliary loss relative to the task loss. Assignment counts are discrete, while the probability averages provide a differentiable path. This specific form is only one design; other routers use different balancing mechanisms.
issues.after: A common top-one balancing term uses f_e, the fraction of tokens assigned to expert e, and P_e, the mean routing probability for e across the batch. The product sum penalizes concentration when assignment frequency and probability mass align. Let N_E denote the number of experts. A coefficient λ sets the strength of this auxiliary loss relative to the task loss. Assignment counts are discrete, while the probability averages provide a differentiable path. This specific form is only one design; other routers use different balancing mechanisms.
issues.reason: Define expert count and explicit loss coefficient without overloading the expert-function symbol.
issues.origin: Claude baseline finding validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: A rough estimate for dense Transformer training is C ≈ 6ND, with N parameters and D training tokens, ignoring important architecture- and sequence-dependent overheads. Under fixed C, doubling N roughly halves the affordable D in this approximation. The best balance depends on how loss responds to both capacity and data. Compute-optimal training also differs from deployment-optimal design: a smaller model trained longer may be attractive when inference will be repeated many times.
issues.after: A rough estimate for dense Transformer training is C ≈ 6ND, with N parameters and D training tokens, ignoring important architecture- and sequence-dependent overheads. In Kaplan et al., N counts non-embedding parameters and the estimate omits context-dependent attention FLOPs. Check each study's parameter-count and compute conventions before comparing allocation rules. Under fixed C, doubling N roughly halves the affordable D in this approximation. The best balance depends on how loss responds to both capacity and data. Compute-optimal training also differs from deployment-optimal design: a smaller model trained longer may be attractive when inference will be repeated many times.
issues.reason: Specify Kaplan's non-embedding parameter and context-dependent-compute conventions.
issues.origin: Expanded Claude finding independently validated by OpenAI audit

Inspect paired disagreements, uncertainty, prompt and sampling variation, and whether either model used the test set for selection. A broader or repeated evaluation may show that the difference is unstable.

issues.before: Take d_in = 8, d_out = 6, and r = 2. Full matrix adaptation has 48 trainable values; the two adapter matrices have 16 + 12 = 28. A high rank is not necessarily parameter-efficient for tiny layers. Test the implementation by comparing the two-path output with the output of an explicitly merged matrix using fixed weights and dropout disabled. The outputs should agree within numerical tolerance, and frozen W should receive no parameter gradient.
issues.after: Take d_in = 8, d_out = 6, and r = 2. Full matrix adaptation has 48 trainable values; the two adapter matrices have 16 + 12 = 28, a saving. The break-even rank is d_in d_out/(d_in + d_out) = 48/14 ≈ 3.43. Rank 4 would require 56 adapter values, exceeding the full matrix's 48. Tiny layers leave little room for parameter-efficient ranks. Test the implementation by comparing the two-path output with the output of an explicitly merged matrix using fixed weights and dropout disabled. The outputs should agree within numerical tolerance, and frozen W should receive no parameter gradient.
issues.reason: Use the same dimensions to show both a saving rank and an inefficient rank.
issues.origin: Expanded Claude finding independently validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: For rsLoRA, the adapter multiplier is α/√r. With α = 16 and r = 64, that multiplier is 2; standard α/r would be 0.25. For a conceptual DoRA weight vector, write w′ = m(v + Δv)/‖v + Δv‖. The normalization isolates a direction, while m controls length. Actual matrix implementations must specify which axis defines a weight vector and how norms are computed. A zero or tiny norm needs numerically careful handling.
issues.after: For rsLoRA, the adapter multiplier is α/√r. With α = 16 and r = 64, that multiplier is 2; standard α/r would be 0.25. For a conceptual DoRA weight vector, write w′ = m(v + Δv)/‖v + Δv‖. The normalization isolates a direction, while m controls length. Actual matrix implementations must specify which axis defines a weight vector and how norms are computed. A zero or tiny norm needs numerically careful handling. In the paper's matrix convention, V starts at W₀ and m at W₀'s column norms, so zero BA preserves the initial weight for nonzero columns. Its memory-saving variant detaches the norm denominator from backpropagation while recomputing its value in each forward pass. The forward expression is unchanged, but the gradients differ.
issues.reason: Primary DoRA text specifies pretrained column-norm magnitude initialization and a detached-denominator memory-saving variant.
issues.origin: Expanded Claude finding independently validated by OpenAI audit

issues.before: Prepare tokenized examples with appropriate labels and padding masks. For causal language modeling, decide whether loss covers all text or only the desired response tokens; the choice affects the learning objective. Run a single batch first, inspect the loss, and verify that adapter gradients are finite and nonzero after an appropriate initialization step. Check that the optimizer contains only intended parameters. Quantized workflows also require the supported preparation steps for the installed PEFT and Transformers versions.
issues.after: Prepare tokenized examples with appropriate labels and padding masks. For causal language modeling, decide whether loss covers all text or only the desired response tokens; the choice affects the learning objective. Run a single batch first and inspect the loss. With standard random-A, zero-B initialization, the task-loss gradient for A is zero on the first backward pass; B can receive a nonzero gradient. After B changes, gradients can reach A. Check finite gradients and the expected pattern for the actual initialization, data, and objective, rather than requiring every tensor to be nonzero. Check that the optimizer contains only intended parameters. Quantized workflows also require the supported preparation steps for the installed PEFT and Transformers versions.
issues.reason: State the initial LoRA gradient pattern explicitly without promising nonzero B or later A gradients for degenerate data/loss cases.

Added preservation of top-k membership and possible change to nucleus membership under positive temperature scaling, with operation-order reporting. Verified independently by a numerical example.

The version-pinned PEFT v0.21.0 URL resolves and documents rank_pattern, initialization, and relevant LoRA behavior. No installed PEFT environment is prescribed by these conceptual articles, and the text already asks readers to record versions. Unversioning a verified reference would reduce specificity.

Made zero-based indexing explicit and added second/third ordinal positions in the answer.
The original unscaled statistic was mathematically valid, but N_E and an explicit lambda-weighted total loss remove symbol and scaling ambiguity.
Verified GShard's full-text AllToAll and dispatch discussion, added the reference, and connected the paper-reading section to token/expert resharding.

Independent audit had already qualified the all-channel claim to ungrouped convolution and cited official grouped/depthwise documentation; CPU examples also checked standard and depthwise parameter counts.

limitations: Reference identity was verified for every citation; targeted full-text passages were inspected for specialist claims, not every page of all 45 sources.

Other modules' article contents were outside this audit; prerequisite IDs were checked structurally across the repository.
Independent audit snippets ran in a local CPU environment and validate toy arithmetic/algebra, not production performance.

dispositions.reason: Verified Sennrich's within-word merges and boundary markers, and SentencePiece's explicit normalized-text reconstruction contract. Replaced the ambiguous exercise. Did not adopt the suggestion of universally lossless raw-text reconstruction or unrestricted cross-whitespace merges: normalization and segmentation settings matter.

Kaplan's primary text excludes embeddings from N and omits context-dependent attention costs in its 6N-per-token estimate. Added these conventions and instructed readers to compare each study's accounting rather than assuming identical parameter definitions.

The accuracy gap is a net correct-answer difference; the number of paired disagreements can be much larger. Added a concrete 10-versus-9 discordance example. Did not add a standalone binomial-standard-error or named-test prescription because the existing paired-analysis guidance suffices and avoids implying independent-model uncertainty.

The original rank-2 example saves parameters; added the exact break-even threshold and rank-4 counterexample for the same layer. Independently verified 48/14 = 3.42857..., rank-2 count 28, and rank-4 count 56.

DoRA's primary text initializes V=W0 and magnitudes from column norms, then documents a memory-saving detached-denominator variant. Added both, qualified initial reconstruction to nonzero norm columns, and emphasized that detachment preserves forward values while changing gradients. CPU autograd checks confirmed the distinction.

Made the standard zero-B first-backward pattern explicit: task-loss gradient for A is zero, B can receive gradients, and A can receive gradients after B changes. Did not adopt guarantees that B or later A must be nonzero. Verified both a nondegenerate two-step case and a zero-input counterexample.

expandedExternalReview.limitations: Claude's expanded review was reasoning-only; source claims and proposed edits were independently checked by OpenAI. Two suggestions required qualifications to avoid raw-text-losslessness and guaranteed-nonzero-gradient overstatements.
